opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the thing that struck me most was how technical he is. You hear about CEOs of companies that size and you assume they're mostly operating at the level of strategy and partnerships, but he was really engaged with the details: how people are actually building with these models, what the data infrastructure underneath looks like, where things break in production. He asked good follow-up questions and clearly thinks about this stuff a lot.

The other thing was how much he frames AI as a platform shift, not just a feature. He's lived through a few of these at Microsoft, client-server, then cloud, and he thinks a lot about what the new stack looks like and where the value ends up. That lines up with how we think about it at Databricks: models matter a lot, but so do the data, the governance, and the tooling around them. A lot of what enterprises actually struggle with is everything around the model.

He was also very gracious and calm, which I think says something about how he runs things. It didn't feel like a scripted keynote moment. It felt like a real conversation between people who care about the same problems. I came away pretty impressed.

r001.rationale: Matei describes Nadella as deeply engaged with technical details, data infrastructure, and production problems, then says his platform view aligns with how Databricks thinks about AI. This conveys the Databricks-CEO-like impression.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, what struck me most was how technical he still is. You go into a conversation like that expecting the CEO version, where everything gets rounded up to strategy and market talk, and instead he wanted to get into the details. He was asking about how people actually use open source data formats, how Spark and lakehouse architectures evolved, what happens when agents start querying data directly instead of humans writing SQL. He clearly reads a lot and talks to engineers, and it shows.

The second thing was how much he framed everything around the end user getting value, not around Microsoft winning. He had this line about how the measure of success for AI should be whether it shows up in GDP numbers, whether a nurse or a small business owner actually gets more done. For someone running a company of that size, that is a pretty grounded way to think about it, and it matched how he talked about partnerships. He was very comfortable saying that Microsoft would not build everything itself.

And he is very calm. There was a lot going on at that Build, a lot of noise around the industry, and he was unhurried, listening, asking follow-up questions. I came away thinking that the culture shift people credit him with is not a PR story. You can feel it in a one-on-one conversation.

r001.rationale: The response describes Nadella as technically engaged and interested in Spark and lakehouse architectures, but it never says he sounded more like a Databricks CEO.
